title: Checkpoint: Faith and Empire
objective: After this level you can explain how faith shaped art from Byzantium to Gothic Europe and the Islamic world.
summary: Hagia Sophia, built as Justinian's church in 532–537, became a mosque in 1453, a museum from 1934 and a mosque in 2020: its mosaics and calligraphy carry the whole chapter.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: one building, a church, a mosque, a museum, a mosque again.
cards.body: Hagia Sophia, in Istanbul, holds this whole chapter under one dome: Byzantine gold, Islamic calligraphy and the question of what belongs in a place of prayer. First, the chapter in order.

events.label: Justinian and Theodora in gold at Ravenna
Fan Kuan's mountain and mule train

cards.fact: Hagia Sophia was built as a church in just five years, 532 to 537.
cards.context: Justinian, the emperor from Level 21's mosaic, built it in Constantinople. When the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II conquered the city in 1453, it became a mosque: minarets went up outside, and many figural mosaics were plastered over. In 1934 it was made a museum, and in 2020 a mosque again.

cards.headline: Two faiths, one dome
cards.body: Plastering over the mosaics followed Level 22's rule: mosques don't show people. In the 19th century, huge round panels of Arabic calligraphy, naming God, Muhammad and the early caliphs, were hung inside. In the 1930s, many mosaics were uncovered again. Today the gold saints and the great written names share the same space, each tradition saying in its own way what is holy.

mascot.line: Same walls, two answers to one question: how do you show the holy? Worth a slow look.

questions.prompt: What happened to Hagia Sophia after the Ottoman conquest of 1453?

options.label: It was pulled down and rebuilt
options.rationale: The building survived; its use changed.

options.label: It was abandoned for centuries
options.rationale: It stayed in use as a mosque.

questions.explanation: After Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453, Hagia Sophia became a mosque, with minarets added.

questions.prompt: Why were many of Hagia Sophia's mosaics plastered over once it became a mosque?

options.label: The gold was taken to pay for the war
options.rationale: The mosaics were covered, not stripped.

options.label: Mosques keep images of people out of prayer spaces
The mosaics had been damaged in a fire
options.rationale: It was a religious choice, not repair.

options.label: Plaster made the dome stronger
options.rationale: The reason was belief, not engineering.

questions.explanation: Islamic religious spaces avoid images of people, so the figural mosaics were covered.

questions.prompt: Chapter recap: which of these came first?
questions.explanation: Justinian and Theodora at San Vitale date to about 547, the earliest of these.

questions.prompt: From Level 27: what gave medieval stained glass its color?

options.label: Paint brushed onto clear glass
options.rationale: Paint added details; the color was in the glass.

options.label: Colored lead between the pieces
options.rationale: Lead joined the pieces; it didn't color them.

options.label: Metal oxides added to the molten glass
Sunlight passing through dyed cloth
options.rationale: The color is in the glass itself.

questions.explanation: Glassmakers added metal oxides, such as cobalt for blue, to the molten glass.

questions.prompt: From Level 23: what does the name Alhambra mean?

options.label: The palace of lions
options.rationale: The lions are in one courtyard, not the name.

options.label: The victory of God
options.rationale: That's close to the Nasrid motto, not the name.

questions.explanation: Alhambra comes from Arabic al-Hamra, "the red one", after its reddish walls.
